tldr: Simply adding tactile future prediction to a world-action model is not enough; by introducing "TacPAC," which caches the predicted contact states and compares them against actual tactile feedback to correct actions in real time, the success rate on real-robot tasks can be dramatically improved.

(a) Contact examples across real-robot tasks; (b) the overall pipeline of future prediction and action planning with a world-action model alongside asynchronous real-time correction by a tactile expert; (c) the core idea of comparing "what was anticipated" against "what was actually felt"; (d) task success rate comparisons from ablation studies.
overview:
For tasks involving delicate physical contact—such as plugging in a charging cable or picking up fragile potato chips—camera images alone miss tiny misalignments, slips, and local surface deformations, leading to failures. To address this, integrating tactile sensor information into robot action control has attracted substantial attention.

A recent trend is World-Action Models (WAMs), which plan robot actions while simultaneously predicting future observations resulting from those actions. It is tempting to think: "Why not just treat tactile images as an extra camera view and predict them into the future as well?" However, experiments reveal that doing so naively recovers only about one-third of the achievable performance gain. The root cause is a timing mismatch: action planning occurs before execution, whereas tactile feedback arrives during execution. Once an action chunk (a sequence of planned movements) is generated, it cannot be adapted if unexpected contact occurs mid-execution.

To bridge this gap, the authors developed "TacPAC." The key idea is to retain the predicted contact state and the plan's internal representation as a KV cache when generating the action chunk. During execution, as newly observed tactile images arrive, a lightweight "tactile expert" reads them against that cache to output real-time delta actions for the unexecuted steps. Instead of interpreting touch in isolation, the robot evaluates how the incoming feedback deviates from what it originally anticipated.

Evaluated on five demanding real-robot contact tasks, TacPAC overwhelmingly outperformed a vision-only baseline (22% success rate) as well as a purely predictive tactile model, achieving an average success rate of 64%. The correction takes only 30.4 ms—over 20 times faster than regenerating the entire action chunk.
contributions: Identified a fundamental structural limitation in world-action models: naively predicting future tactile observations fails to incorporate execution-time contact feedback, forfeiting the majority of potential performance gains.

Proposed TacPAC, a framework that caches anticipated contact states and action representations from planning time as attention caches, cross-referencing incoming tactile observations against this cache to correct unexecuted actions on the fly.
Designed a lightweight tactile expert that runs 20.7 times faster than full chunk regeneration (30.4 ms per correction), enabling smooth real-time tracking without stalling the robot's motion.

Demonstrated on five real-robot tasks (including plug insertion and chip handling) that TacPAC achieves an average success rate of 64%, significantly outperforming strong existing VLAs and world-action models, and validated each design component through ablations.

sections.heading: Why is "predicting" touch simply not enough?
sections.summary: Tactile feedback is critical for contact-rich manipulation, but naively having world-action models predict future tactile images yields limited gains. Predictions happen before execution, whereas contact feedback arrives during execution. TacPAC caches the predicted contact from the plan and compares it against live touch to correct actions in real time.
sections.details:
In tasks where contact decides success or failure—such as precision plug insertion or handling fragile potato chips—external cameras cannot fully capture finger deformation, slipping, or minute misalignments. This is where tactile sensors become indispensable.

Recently, World-Action Models (WAMs) that generate action chunks (blocks of multiple action steps) while predicting future observation images have shown strong results. However, prior models have been predominantly vision-centric. A natural next step is to treat tactile images as just another camera angle and predict them into the future, an approach tried in earlier works. Yet the authors found through experiments that this straightforward extension recovers only about a third of the potential gain that tactile feedback could provide.

Why does this happen? There are two main reasons. First, meaningful tactile transitions occur over very brief temporal windows, so standard video prediction loss tends to be insensitive to these critical contact moments. Second, and more fundamentally, there is a "timing mismatch." Predictions happen before actions are executed, while tactile feedback arrives during execution. Once an action chunk is finalized, it cannot be adjusted if unexpected contact occurs during execution.

TacPAC was proposed to resolve this dilemma. At planning time, the model caches the state representing "if I execute this plan, this is the contact I should feel." As new tactile images arrive during execution, it cross-references them against that cache. This enables the policy to instantly determine "how does this differ from the anticipated contact?" and output real-time residual corrections (delta actions) for the remaining unexecuted actions.

captions.F1: Summary of TacPAC's core principle and experimental results. By performing action corrections based on comparing predicted contact states with actual tactile observations, it achieves significantly higher task success rates compared to tactile prediction alone (w/o Tactile Correction) or omitting tactile prediction entirely (w/o Tactile Prediction).

sections.heading: At the crossroads of world-action models and tactile robotics
sections.summary: Existing world-action models are mostly vision-centric, while tactile approaches have historically split between open-loop single-pass planning and purely reactive correction without foresight. TacPAC bridges both worlds by retaining planning-time predictions and cross-referencing them against execution-time feedback.
sections.details:
### Trends in World-Action Models (WAMs)
World-action models predict how actions will alter the future environment and use these predictions as a prior to guide action generation. Approaches include embedding actions directly into diffusion latent spaces or coupling vision and action tokens using Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architectures (such as LingBot-VA). However, almost all of these focus exclusively on vision, leaving them unable to predict or perceive the exact moment of physical contact or slip.

### Tactile Manipulation and Predictive Models
Tactile manipulation in robotics historically centered around immediate feedback based on current sensor measurements, such as tactile servoing and compliance control. More recently, feeding tactile inputs into Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models has gained traction.

Even more recently, studies have started integrating touch into predictive models. However, prior work like Dream-Tac predicts contact in advance but commits to an action chunk in a single forward pass, leaving no room for execution-time adjustment. Conversely, systems like T-Rex can correct actions from an ongoing tactile stream, but lack tactile future prediction; without an internal reference for what contact was expected, they can only react reflexively.

TacPAC's innovation lies in saving the predicted contact information as attention Key/Value caches and reading newly arrived tactile images against this cache. This ability to "compare against expectations" is crucial: experimental ablations show that simply removing access to this cache drops task success rates by 17 percentage points.

sections.heading: Caching predictions for real-time correction: how TacPAC works
sections.summary: TacPAC consists of a base model for video prediction and action planning, alongside a tactile expert that references the cached plan to adjust unexecuted steps. After flow-matching generation, predicted contact and action representations are cached, allowing incoming tactile frames to instantly trigger delta actions.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Problem Formulation and Base Model
TacPAC takes as input language instructions, current camera observations, proprioception (joint states), and tactile sensor images. Tactile images are concatenated with external camera views into a single video latent representation. Using Conditional Flow Matching, future visual/tactile observations and an action chunk (horizon $H=48$) are generated simultaneously.

The architecture relies on a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) design, coupling a video expert that generates frames with an action expert that produces actions. An asymmetric attention mask allows action queries to attend to all video and action tokens, whereas video queries only attend to video tokens. This prevents noisy early action iterates from corrupting observation predictions, while ensuring actions are firmly conditioned on the predicted contact states.

### 3.2 Prediction-Conditioned Tactile Correction (Cache & Expert)
Once the base model finishes generating an action chunk $\hat{\mathbf{a}}$, a single forward pass is run at the noise-free state (flow time $\tau=0$) to store the attention Keys and Values from each layer as a cache $\mathcal{C}$. Specifically, only the "predicted tactile tokens" and "planned action tokens" are cached. Background visual tokens change minimally over the chunk and are excluded, saving both memory and computation.

When the robot executes $m$ steps into the plan, a new tactile image $\mathbf{I}_m$ arrives. The tactile expert uses this image and the updated action chunk (where the $m$ executed steps are replaced by the actual sent actions, and unexecuted steps keep their planned values) as queries. By referencing cache $\mathcal{C}$, it produces residual corrections (delta actions $\Delta\mathbf{a}$) for the remaining unexecuted steps in a single forward pass.

### 3.3 Training and Inference
Training is conducted in two stages:
- **Stage 1 (Base Model Training)**: The video and action experts are trained jointly using conditional flow-matching loss.
- **Stage 2 (Tactile Expert Training)**: The Stage 1 weights are completely frozen, and only the tactile expert is trained. The frozen base model plans actions, various execution offsets $m$ are sampled, and the expert is trained via supervised learning to predict the residual difference between the remaining plan and ground-truth demonstrations. This trains the expert specifically to correct the base model's planning biases.

At inference time, as soon as the base model outputs an action chunk, execution begins immediately while cache generation runs concurrently in the background. Whenever a new tactile frame arrives, the tactile expert asynchronously computes corrections and updates the unexecuted actions starting just after the current step.

captions.F2: Overview of the TacPAC architecture. In Stage 1, the video expert and action expert are trained for future prediction and action planning. In Stage 2, those weights are frozen, and the tactile expert is trained to output real-time delta actions by referencing the KV cache of predicted contact and action tokens.

sections.heading: Evaluated on five real-robot tasks: high success rates and 30 ms corrections
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted on five real-robot tasks, including plug insertion and chip transfer. TacPAC achieved an average success rate of 64%, well above the strongest baseline (48%). Ablations confirmed the vital roles of prediction, correction, and the cache, while correction latency was clocked at just 30.4 ms.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup and Tasks
Experiments were conducted on a Flexiv Rizon 4 arm equipped with two InTac S1 tactile sensors on the gripper fingers, alongside wrist-mounted and third-person RealSense cameras. The evaluation covered five tasks:
- Charger plug insertion into a wall socket (precision alignment)
- Sequential transfer of three fruits into a tray (grasp force regulation and multi-stage execution)
- Fragile potato chip transfer (delicate force control without breaking)
- Standing up a fallen empty plastic bottle (grasping and reorienting a lightweight, easily deformable object)
- Motherboard expansion card insertion (high-precision alignment and insertion force)

Each task was evaluated over 20 real-robot trials. Baselines included the generalist VLA model $\pi_{0.5}$, ACT (imitation learning), VITaL (reactive tactile policy), LingBot-VA (visual world-action model), as well as Dream-Tac and T-Rex (tactile world-action models).

### 4.2 Results and Analysis (Q1)
TacPAC ranked first across all five tasks, achieving an overall average success rate of 64%. This surpasses the best baseline, T-Rex (48%), by 16 percentage points, and nearly triples the visual-only base WAM (22%).

Dream-Tac and T-Rex exhibited complementary failure modes. Dream-Tac, which relies solely on advance prediction, performed well on tasks requiring immediate, correct initial force such as "Chips" (85%) and "Fruits" (40%), but struggled on "Plug Insertion" (55%) where continuous correction is required. Conversely, T-Rex, with real-time corrections, did well on plug insertion (65%) but failed on chips (75%) because it lacked an initial force prior; once a chip was crushed, recovery was impossible. By unifying both—correcting against an anticipated baseline—TacPAC led in both categories, reaching 90% on chips and 80% on plug insertion.

### 4.3 Ablation Studies and Latency (Q2–Q4)
- **Q2 (Why prediction alone is insufficient)**: Data diagnostics revealed that contact transition frames containing meaningful tactile changes account for only 4.9% of all frames; video prediction loss is dominated by static frames. The prediction-only variant (w/o tactile expert) reached only a 37% success rate, capturing only about a third of the full gain.
- **Q3 (Component contributions)**: Disabling the cache reference (w/o tactile cache) dropped performance sharply to 47%. With the exact same model size and tactile inputs, the ability to "compare against anticipated contact" accounted for a 17-point margin.
- **Q4 (Real-time capability)**: The tactile expert's computation latency was only 30.4 ms (operating at 32.9 Hz). This is 20.7 times faster than full action chunk regeneration, allowing it to easily keep pace with the robot's 30 Hz control loop.

sections.heading: Conclusion: predict contact, then act against expectations
sections.summary: TacPAC dramatically elevates contact-rich manipulation by combining world-action model tactile prediction with expectation-conditioned real-time action corrections. Prediction and correction complement each other, offering a robust paradigm for closed-loop robotic control.
sections.details:
This work introduced TacPAC, a tactile world-action model designed for challenging contact-rich manipulation.

By overcoming the limitation of prior methods that lock in actions before execution, TacPAC caches the contact states anticipated during planning and updates unexecuted action steps asynchronously at high frequency by comparing live tactile observations against that cache.

In real-robot experiments across five contact-rich tasks, TacPAC outperformed existing state-of-the-art baselines across the board, boosting the average success rate from 22% (vision-only base) to 64%. The correction module is exceptionally fast, requiring only 30.4 ms per pass.

Ultimately, predicting touch beforehand and reacting to touch on the fly are not mutually exclusive; they are complementary. Designing policies that correct actions based on "what differed from expectations" provides an effective blueprint for delicate, responsive physical interaction.

sections.heading: Appendix: implementation details and experimental setup
sections.summary: This section summarizes model architecture parameters (Transformer dimensions, flow-matching settings), physical setup, and evaluation protocols, along with diagnostic details showing that contact transitions drive the majority of tactile variation.
sections.details:
### Model Architecture and Training Setup
The video, action, and tactile experts all share a 30-layer Transformer architecture with identical attention geometry (24 heads, head dimension 128). This shared geometry allows the tactile expert to directly read the KV cache of the base model. The action chunk horizon is $H=48$ (7-DoF relative joint angles plus 1-DoF gripper state); at a 30 Hz control rate, one chunk corresponds to 1.6 seconds of motion.

During Stage 2 training, $K=4$ execution offsets are sampled for each base model plan to compute an averaged loss, improving training efficiency. Training was conducted on a node with 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs, using a global batch size of 64 for 10 epochs.

### Robot Setup and Task Protocols
The setup utilized a Flexiv Rizon 4 arm with InTac S1 sensors mounted on the gripper fingers. Reset routines, object placements, trial counts (20 per task), and binary success criteria were strictly standardized across all methods:
- **Plug Insertion**: Success requires full seating of the charger plug into the socket.
- **Fruit Transfer**: Sequential transfer of all three fruits into the tray without surface damage.
- **Chip Transfer**: Transporting a fragile potato chip to the target plate without crushing or cracking it.
- **Bottle Uprighting**: Lifting a fallen empty bottle to an upright stance; counted as success if it remains standing after release.
- **Expansion Card Insertion**: Full engagement of the card edge connector into the motherboard slot.

### Contact Data Diagnostics for Q2
Tactile change magnitude $c_t$ was measured across motion phases defined by gripper velocity. While "contact transition windows" (where the fingers first touch objects) accounted for only 4.9% of all frames, they contained 18.6% of all tactile variation. This indicates a variation rate more than four times higher than during steady periods, explaining why conventional video prediction losses overlook these brief but critical events.

takeaways: Treating touch merely as an additional camera view in world-action models discards most achievable gains due to temporal mismatches and the sparsity of contact events.
Caching "what contact was anticipated" during action planning and cross-referencing incoming tactile feedback against that cache enables meaningful, high-precision action corrections.
Performing a lightweight, single-pass correction over the attention cache—rather than re-planning the full chunk—achieves real-time adjustment in about 30 ms (over 20x faster).
Prior force anticipation and runtime error correction are complementary: uniting them allows a policy to handle both fragile objects and tight mechanical insertions reliably.
limitations: Because the tactile expert only attends to the cached plan and current tactile inputs, it cannot easily accommodate large visual scene changes or dynamic visual disturbances occurring mid-chunk.
Regenerating action chunks with the base model (re-planning) still incurs a latency of several hundred milliseconds, precluding instant large-scale horizon shifts.

All physical evaluations were conducted on a single robot platform (Flexiv Rizon 4 with specific tactile sensors); generalizability across diverse sensor morphologies and multi-arm setups remains open for future study.
